title: EU Banks’ AML Algorithms Flag Minority Names in 61.8% of Alerts, Audit Finds
excerpt: By Kyle Belmonte Published: Oct 16 2026, 8:43 AM EDT. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on Pocket. Dutch civil liberties group Privacy First warned Thursday that the European Union's new Anti-Money Laundering Authority is preparing continent-wide bank screening guidelines that risk encoding a documented pattern of algorithmic discrimination into every bank account across 27 member states — a pattern a government audit has now confirmed in the Netherlands, where people with foreign-sounding surnames appeared in 61. 8% of suspicious-transaction reports examined by national auditors. The warning, reported Thursday by civil-liberties monitor Statewatch , comes as AMLA finalizes binding guidelines under Article 26(5) of the Anti-Money Laundering Regulation (AMLR) — a framework that will require banks, accountants, crypto-asset providers, and other "obliged entities" to run continuous algorithmic monitoring of their customers' financial behavior starting July 10, 2027. What AMLA's Draft Guidelines Require. AMLA describes its approach to bank customer screening as "technology-neutral": monitoring may be manual, automated, or semi-automated, provided that whatever method a firm uses is explainable, regularly tested, properly documented, and proportionate to its size and risk exposure. The AMLA Art. 26(5) consultation paper simultaneously invites firms to consider whether algorithms, machine learning, and artificial intelligence might sharpen their ability to detect money-laundering indicators. The proposed safeguards include: avenues for customers to appeal decisions, requirements for human oversight of automated outputs, and obligations on firms to ensure their tools do not produce discriminatory results. Banks must also be able to explain their systems and their conclusions to supervisors on request. Privacy First, a Dutch civil liberties foundation, submitted a formal AMLA consultation response to AMLA on September 2, 2026. In it, the organization argued that those safeguards remain insufficient to prevent what it calls the risk of the EU becoming "a financial surveillance state in which" citizens' financial lives are subject to opaque algorithmic scrutiny. Dutch Testing Ground: A Government Audit Found 61. 8% Minority-Name Flagging. Privacy First describes the Netherlands as "a testing ground" for AML controls in Europe — and the Dutch data gives regulators a measurable preview of what a scaled-up regime produces. Dutch banks reported nearly 250,000 unusual transactions to the national Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-NL) in 2020. By 2024, that figure had more than doubled to more than 530,000. Eight major Dutch banks deployed approximately 13,000 full-time-equivalent staff on AML work in 2024 at a combined cost of approximately €1. 6 billion (approximately $1. 8 billion USD; exchange rate as of October 15, 2026; conversions are approximate) — a compliance burden banks routinely pass on to customers through higher fees. Yet a landmark Court of Audit review published March 11, 2026, by the Netherlands Court of Audit found that available information provided no meaningful insight into whether any of those expenditures actually detected money laundering. Of 217 suspicious-activity reports the auditors examined, 61. 8% involved a person with a foreign-sounding surname — an overrepresentation the court said "could not be explained" by any documented risk factor and "may be indicative of discrimination. " The same review found that mosques were questioned more often about the purpose and source of their transactions than the Catholic and Protestant institutions in the sample. The ING Bank case makes the pattern concrete. In mid-2024, the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights ruled against ING after two customers discovered their transactions had been repeatedly blocked or delayed because their names did not sound Dutch. title: Self Labs Launches Agent Vault as Banks Lock AI Agents Out of Accounts
excerpt: Agent Vault went live on October 15, built on the bet that AI agents will eventually need to log into accounts and pay on a person's behalf. Banks spent the same week telling investors that's exactly the door they're not opening. Self Labs launched Agent Vault on October 15. It's a credential and payments layer that lets AI agents sign into accounts and complete purchases on a person's behalf, without the agent ever seeing the underlying card number or password. According to a release carried by Business Wire and reported by outlets including 01net and Le Lezard, the product holds a user's payment and login credentials in one vault. It injects them into a transaction only at the moment an agent needs to act, so the agent itself never stores or transmits the raw data. Self says Agent Vault already connects to the AI assistants people are actually using day to day, including Muse, OpenClaw, Hermes, Grok Bot, Claude and Codex. The timing is not a coincidence so much as a bet. Two days before Self's launch, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call that the bank will not let outside AI agents operate inside customer accounts. "We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon said, according to reporting from Banking Dive and PYMNTS. A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to reporters that the bank currently blocks third-party agents from taking action on behalf of retail customers. That includes Meta's Muse and the AI agent Instinct, whose maker reportedly reached a $10 billion valuation last month. No timeline for changing that. JPMorgan still allows read-only account access through connectors like Plaid. It just won't let an outside agent actually move money. That is precisely the gap Agent Vault is built to sit in front of. If a bank's objection is that it can't verify who, or what, is initiating a transaction, Self has a direct answer: a vault that strips the agent of any ability to see or exfiltrate the credential in the first place. That's the liability question Dimon raised on that earnings call, the one about who's responsible when a rogue or hijacked agent misuses access. Self isn't alone in building this kind of credential broker. Infisical runs an open-source version that routes an agent's API calls through a proxy which attaches real credentials only on the way out, and Crossmint has its own PCI-compliant vault for agent cards. But Self is the one explicitly pitching itself at the exact moment a Wall Street bank is making the opposite argument in public. Self Labs isn't a fintech newcomer improvising its way into payments. The company built its name on zero-knowledge identity verification. It raised a $9 million seed round in November 2025 from Greenfield Capital, Startup Capital Ventures's fund with SBI, Spearhead VC and a list of angel backers that includes Casey Neistat and EigenLayer's Sreeram Kannan. In April 2026 it acquired Loam, an agentic-workflow startup founded by Birju Shah, Uber's former head of AI, bringing Shah on as chief operating officer specifically to build out Self's identity stack for autonomous agents. Agent Vault is the first product to come out of that combination, six months later. Natural raised $30 million to give AI agents their own bank accounts Natural, a payments startup founded in 2025, raised a $30 million Series A led by Forerunner Ventures just 193 days after starting, pushing its total funding past $40 million. The company launched six products, including FDIC-insured Wallets for AI agents, positioning itself as a direct challenger to Stripe. - AI agents with bank accounts - giving AI agents spending power. The pricing says a lot about who Self thinks will adopt this first. The free tier gives a user one agent card and five payments a month: barely enough to run an errand. title: FCA plans to automate supervision and enforcement using AI
excerpt: FCA plans to automate supervision and enforcement using AI. By Jonathan Easton 16/10/2026. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) plans to use artificial intelligence to automate much of its supervision and enforcement work, while holding off on introducing new AI-specific rules for financial services firms. Jessica Rusu, the FCA's chief data, information and intelligence officer, told MPs on Tuesday that the regulator wants to expand its use of AI to analyse emails, documents and interview records submitted by regulated firms. The approach forms part of plans to develop an AI-enabled supervisory model that allows officials to identify potential risks and intervene at scale. Rusu said the FCA wants to go “further than that, to automate wherever we can. and to intervene at scale”. The regulator is exploring applications across authorisations, supervision and enforcement, with human officials retaining oversight of decisions. Chief executive Nikhil Rathi told the House of Commons Treasury Committee that the FCA is not yet convinced it needs significantly greater powers to regulate AI. Rathi said he wanted the watchdog to demonstrate that it had used its existing powers to their fullest extent before seeking more. The debate extends to whether general-purpose AI models such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini should fall within financial services regulation. Rathi said chatbots providing general information, rather than personalised recommendations that lead to transactions, do not currently fall fully within the regulated perimeter. “I think that is going to be a very live discussion,” Rathi told MPs, referring to where the regulatory boundary should be drawn. The question follows the July Mills Review, led by former FCA executive Sheldon Mills, which recommended an AI-enabled supervisory model and called for consideration of whether large language models should be subject to financial rules. Research commissioned for the review found that one-fifth of UK adults would be open to allowing AI models to make financial decisions for them, including decisions involving savings and borrowing, according to the Financial Times. The FCA is already testing AI applications. Its AI Live Testing service opened in December 2025, with NatWest, Monzo, Santander and Scottish Widows among the first participants. The regulator has also worked with the Monetary Authority of Singapore on testing AI tools and previously provided banks with access to NVIDIA computing resources through a sandbox initiative. Rusu said the FCA would publish findings on good and poor AI practices at financial services firms the following week, alongside its response to the growing use of advanced AI models. The regulator's approach currently relies on existing frameworks, including Consumer Duty, rather than a separate set of AI-specific requirements. Share Story:.

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
excerpt: Business News and Finance. Markets Business Investing Tech Politics Select Make It. Finance. Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos. Published Wed, Oct 14 2026 2:47 PM EDT Updated Wed, Oct 14 2026 4:06 PM EDT. Hugh Son @hugh_son. WATCH LIVE. KEY POINTS. Bank of America added 1,000 third-party consultants to support 3,000 internal staff in patching proprietary and vendor software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos. Software patching, combined with anti-money laundering compliance, added hundreds of millions in third-quarter costs, which CEO Brian Moynihan expects will decline over time. While defensive patching creates short-term expenses, BofA’s 130 internal AI projects are projected to drive $700 million in savings next year. In this article. BAC. Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos , the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan , told CNBC on Wednesday. In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release , Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker. "We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said. The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U. S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April. They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said. Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time. In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI. title: Colony Bank uses gen AI to shave days off SBA loan approvals
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. Colony Bank uses gen AI to shave days off SBA loan approvals. By Penny Crosman. About Penny. twitter. pennycrosman. mailto. penny. crosman@arizent. com. linkedin. pennycrosman. Published October 16, 2026, 4:16 p. m. EDT. |. Updated October 16, 2026, 4:47 p. m. EDT. 4 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: Using generative AI helped Colony Bank adapt to new SBA rules more readily, according to an executive at the bank. Forward look: The bank plans to start approving larger loans on the platform in a few weeks. When the Small Business Administration announced changes to SBA loan requirements in August, Darren Davis, president of Colony Bank's small-business specialty lending division, estimated the changes would add five days to the time needed to process each loan, on top of the typical 10-day loan approval process. The Trump administration issued 416 pages of revised SBA rules that took effect Oct. 1. The new rules tighten lending criteria, increase documentation requirements and alter business acquisition standards. Processing Content. Davis and other leaders at Georgia-based Colony Bank deployed generative AI-based business loan origination software from Lama AI and were able to reduce the lending process from 92 steps to 32 — a 67% reduction. "Now if the customer's engaged with us and responsive, we're about seven business days," he said. Colony now originates all of its SBA Express loans, along with certain other non-SBA commercial loan products, through Lama AI. In a broader trend, U. S. banks are seeing productivity gains from implementations of AI. In an American Banker survey conducted earlier this year, 41% of respondents said AI integration was the top driver of improved employee productivity over the last 12 months, followed by improved efficiency internally (34%), new tech and tools (25%), task automation (23%) and process simplification (17%). In lending, banks are typically using AI in credit decisions to approve more loans. "If I'm using AI to say no, then that's questionable, especially under issues like fair lending," said Carey Ransom, managing director of BankTech Ventures. At PNC, generative AI is never used to say no on a credit decision, according to Ned Carroll, the bank's head of data and automation. "But I very well might use a generative AI system to say yes more often," he told American Banker in a recent interview. At Colony Bank, generative AI performs data validation and analysis and makes a recommendation that's reviewed by a human. The bank started down this path two years ago. "We had a small working capital program," Davis told American Banker. "We had two different tiers on it — up to $150,000 and up to $350,000 — and we were looking for a system that would allow people to get pre-qualified for one or the other before they went into a full application process, and so that was our initial thought on it. When we saw the robustness of Llama, we started going down a different path. ". The different path was to use Lama as a full loan origination system, rather than just a front-end solution for initial assessments. Davis' team used the software to remove 60 manual tasks from the loan process. "A lot of our information is document reading and verifying what the customer put in versus what's on a document," he said. "A lot of that went away because Lama does that for us. Lama's able to read documents and populate fields, so we know it's coming from the source and it's not being fat-fingered in. We're not having to double-check to make sure people entered things correctly. ". The software compares data provided on loan applications against data from LexisNexis and a third-party business scoring provider to conduct know-your-customer and know-your-business data validations. title: IMF-World Bank meetings focus on global risks and potential benefits of AI
excerpt: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, Governor of the Bank of Canada Tiff Macklem and Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of IMF, attend "AI and the Global Economy: From Risk to Opportunity" at the IMF/World Bank 2026 Annual Meetings at Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok, Thailand, on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by Patipat Janthong/Reuters. IMF-World Bank meetings focus on global risks and potential benefits of AI. By — Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press. World Oct 16, 2026 1:30 PM EDT. BANGKOK (AP) — Guardrails are urgently needed to contain potential risks from the boom in artificial intelligence, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Friday, likening the technology to a Formula 1 race car that might go off the track and run people over. "We are racing, and the question is how do we put barriers? So if a car was to fly out it doesn't kill people," IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said. "I have high respect for the industry. I think what you're doing is incredibly important for humanity. You may give us the biggest gift, but if the car runs over people, that gift may not be so worthwhile," she said while speaking on a panel on the impact of AI on the world economy along with experts including Anthropic co-founder and head of policy Jack Clark. READ MORE: Fed chair Warsh says price stability is key but shies away from signals about rates. Clark is among technology industry leaders pushing for faster action on regulating AI. In a blog post last month, the rival to OpenAI proposed that the world's top artificial intelligence companies come up with a coordinated way to pause development of advanced AI systems, warning the technology is improving so quickly there's a risk humans would lose control. "I think it's worse than you describe. I think it's Formula 1 at night without maybe brakes in the cars," Clark said. "And it's remarkable to me that the toys I buy for my children are regulated more than the literal superintelligence I work on at my day job. ". He added that the effort to build policy frameworks to regulate AI is underway. "The world is now taking this seriously, and I think if we take it seriously, we are going to be able to get our arms around it," Clark said. "But it cannot only be companies making these decisions. And if we're negligent about this, we're going to get some form of chaos. ". The impact of AI on jobs is yet to be fully understood, but an IMF study found three main trends. About 10% of jobs might be transformed or newly created, while work involving repetitive tasks will be gone, Georgieva said. The third category will be service sector jobs generated by people who benefit from the investment boom. "The net impact is positive," she said, though she added that "services don't pay a lot. ". "So you get young people who normally would have gone into professional routine jobs now serving coffee in Starbucks. And that is not what I think young people in the world aspire for," she said. Tiff Macklem, the governor of the Bank of Canada, compared that to the effects on employment from more open trade, which has generated great global wealth and raised millions out of poverty. "Without a system to help them cope with the loss you get a backlash. ". Dozens of people marched in Bangkok on Thursday and Friday in peaceful protests, seeking to draw attention to growing inequality and other frustrations. title: AI Risk Management in Finance: Key Lessons From the FSB’s New Report on Responsible AI
excerpt: AI Risk Management in Finance: Key Lessons From the FSB’s New Report on Responsible AI. By Matt Swayne · 16 October 2026 · 9 min read. Insider Brief. Financial institutions can use AI to improve efficiency and fraud detection, but the Financial Stability Board recommends measuring results, assigning accountability and matching controls to potential risks. Firms should evaluate AI’s full costs and performance, including human review, error correction and ongoing monitoring, before expanding deployment. AI agents require limits on system access and authority, while reliance on outside providers calls for clear contracts, assessment of shared dependencies and tested fallback plans. Artificial intelligence can speed financial work and strengthen fraud detection, but its benefits depend on firms’ ability to measure performance, limit its authority and intervene when it fails. For banks, insurers and investment firms, that makes AI adoption a management decision extending well beyond the choice of a model. A system that produces a credit assessment in minutes may still require substantial review. An agent that completes a task successfully may have taken unauthorized steps along the way. Buying software from several vendors may leave a firm dependent on the same underlying technology provider. Those are among the practical implications of the Financial Stability Board’s (FSB) recent report, “Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence. ” The international body, which coordinates the work of financial authorities and standard-setting organizations, sets out 12 practices covering how institutions select, use and oversee AI. The guidance is nonbinding and does not establish an international standard, but has value for business leaders lies in the questions it provides for evaluating AI investments, assigning responsibility and deciding when automation has earned a larger role. The report also cautions against treating inaction as risk-free, as institutions that fail to adopt AI could become less competitive or less capable of detecting fraud and cyberthreats. The challenge is to identify where AI delivers a measurable improvement and establish controls proportionate to the consequences of failure. A tool that sorts internal documents and a system that influences loan decisions need different levels of scrutiny. Measure the Finished Work. The FSB’s case studies show why speed is an incomplete measure of AI’s value. One medium-sized regional commercial bank used generative AI to extract financial data, prepare credit narratives and support risk detection in small-business lending. Generative AI produces text and other content in response to instructions. The bank reduced the time needed to generate a preliminary credit proposal from more than a day to 15 minutes, according to the report. Yet financial data extraction accuracy was reported as more than 80%, while credit approvers considered more than 70% of the generated content valuable reference material. Those figures describe different aspects of performance. Faster preparation does not establish that every extracted figure is correct or that the proposal is ready for approval. For an institution considering a similar application, this means it’s important is to measure the full process. That includes the time employees spend checking source documents, correcting errors and handling unusual cases, as well as the time saved generating a draft. A useful assessment would track the cost and quality of the completed work. Another case illustrates how responsibilities can be divided. A global asset manager developed an AI application that reviews investment documents and prepares an initial risk assessment linked to relevant rules and source material. It does not approve or reject investments. Accountability remains with the risk manager. That arrangement gives reviewers evidence they can check while directing more of their time toward judgment-intensive work. The FS

title: Agentic AI in Banks Has No US Rulebook: FSB Steps In With Only Framework
excerpt: By Jackie Manning Published: Oct 16 2026, 1:50 AM EDT. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on Pocket. The Financial Stability Board published its final guidance on artificial intelligence Thursday, filling a governance void that American banking regulators had created just six months earlier — when the country's primary model risk management framework was updated to explicitly exclude autonomous AI systems from its scope. OCC Bulletin 2026-13, the interagency guidance issued jointly by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Reserve Board, and the FDIC on April 17, states in plain terms: "Generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving. As such, they are not within the scope of this guidance. " The OCC press release confirmed that exclusion language in full. That sentence created a compliance category without a rulebook. Banks had been deploying autonomous AI in fraud detection, trading, customer service, and loan decisioning — but the governing framework that would otherwise define how those systems must be validated, monitored, and controlled explicitly does not apply to them. The FSB's Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence — 12 non-binding recommended practices released today by the Basel-based body that coordinates financial regulation across G20 economies — is now the only internationally recognized governance document written to address that gap directly. The FSB's final sound practices report carries no enforcement power; compliance is voluntary. In practice, however, FSB sound practices tend to become de facto supervisory benchmarks — particularly in the EU, UK, Singapore, and Japan, where regulators are actively building out their own AI governance regimes and are expected to reference the FSB framework as they do. Read more: Bank AI Oversight Expands to Every Exam: Generative AI Bypasses SR 26-2 as Kill-Switch Gap Grows. What Changed From Consultation Draft to Final Report?. The FSB first circulated a consultation version of the practices on June 10, inviting public comment through July 22. The final document retains the same 12-practice architecture but sharpens two areas in response to industry feedback: autonomous AI oversight and third-party model dependencies. The most significant conceptual addition concerns agentic AI — systems designed to carry out complex, multi-step tasks with limited human intervention. The final guidance clarifies that documentation requirements for autonomous systems are not merely administrative. They must be capable of supporting accountability after the fact: firms must be able to trace and reconstruct the inputs, decisions, and actions of an autonomous system. The FSB's final report on agentic AI added a new case study on agentic AI deployments, along with examples drawn from insurers and non-bank financial firms, to ground the guidance in real-world practice. The FSB also revised Sound Practice 12 — which governs third-party AI risk — to address concerns raised by industry respondents about the opacity of frontier model providers. Updated language now explicitly covers performance monitoring, transparency obligations, business continuity requirements, and exit planning for critical AI services. Institutions are expected to secure contractual rights covering audit access, data portability, security incident notification, and orderly service termination before deploying an externally sourced AI system at material scale. One notable terminological decision: the FSB declined to adopt the framing of AI systems as "synthetic employees," a concept that had surfaced in industry submissions. The board concluded the analogy could obscure that autonomous systems sometimes interpret tasks in ways their human principals never anticipated — a framing it considered too optimistic about machine predictability. title: Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) Deploys Foundry And AIP Platforms Inside Commercial Banking With Customers Bank Deal
excerpt: . Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has agreed to deploy its Foundry and AIP platforms with Customers Bank, targeting AI-led automation of commercial client onboarding workflows. The partnership is designed to streamline document-heavy onboarding processes while preserving what the bank describes as a high-touch client experience for commercial customers. The move represents a meaningful expansion for Palantir beyond its traditional base of government, intelligence, and industrial clients into regulated financial services. Palantir, which carries a reported market value of $482. 9 billion, built its reputation deploying data analytics and orchestration platforms for defense and intelligence agencies worldwide. Applying those same Foundry and AIP tools to commercial banking onboarding is a direct test of whether the company’s AI-first architecture translates into enterprise financial services at scale. The deal places Palantir engineers inside Customers Bank operations, with the goal of rebuilding onboarding workflows from the ground up using the company’s AI platforms. If Palantir can convert a heavily regulated, paperwork-intensive process like commercial onboarding into a reusable Foundry and AIP template, it strengthens the case for repeatable high-value software rollouts in finance. The core commercial thesis for Palantir rests on platforms like Foundry and AIP becoming essential infrastructure for large enterprises, with the private sector gradually taking on more of the growth burden. One unresolved question is whether bank-specific builds of this kind can scale into a broader financial services ecosystem or whether they remain resource-intensive, one-off engineering engagements. Palantir faces established competition in financial workflows from companies like Salesforce and ServiceNow, and must demonstrate that AI-native orchestration rather than bespoke consulting becomes the industry standard. Commercial banking onboarding involves strict regulatory requirements, extensive documentation, and complex risk checks, making it a demanding but high-visibility proving ground for Palantir’s enterprise AI ambitions. A successful and scalable outcome at Customers Bank would provide meaningful evidence that Palantir’s commercial customer base can sustain the kind of rapid enterprise adoption that analysts tracking the stock have pointed to as a key growth driver. title: Die Bank von England warnt vor dem Risiko von Cyberangriffen durch KI.
excerpt: . Die Bank von England warnt vor dem Risiko von Cyberangriffen durch KI. Am 15. Oktober warnte die Bank of England (BoE) die globalen Finanzinstitute, dass sie ausgefeilte Systemwiederherstellungspläne gegen die Bedrohung durch Cyberangriffe mit künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) vorbereiten und ihre Pläne zur Reaktion auf die Risiken, die Quantencomputer für die Sicherheitsstandards der Verschlüsselung darstellen könnten, beschleunigen müssten. Báo Thanh Hóa • 16/10/2026. Sarah Breeden, stellvertretende Gouverneurin der Bank von England für Finanzstabilität, betonte auf der Jahrestagung des Institute of International Finance (IIF) in Bangkok, dass die Entwicklung von KI mittlerweile zu einem „systemischen Risiko“ für die globalen Finanzmärkte geworden sei. Das könnte Sie interessieren. Laut Frau Breeden müssen Banken ihre Sicherheitskapazitäten proaktiv verbessern, anstatt anzunehmen, dass bestehende Schutzmaßnahmen alle Risiken abwehren können. Insbesondere fortschrittliche KI kann ausgenutzt werden, um Schwachstellen in IT-Systemen zu finden und auszunutzen, während autonome KI-Agenten zudem das Risiko bergen, unvorhergesehen zu agieren und bestehende Kontrollmechanismen zu umgehen. Angesichts dieser Situation drängen die britischen Aufsichtsbehörden die größten Banken dazu, „eigenständige Wiederherstellungspläne“ zu erstellen. Dabei handelt es sich um Mechanismen, die auf einer Hardware-Infrastruktur basieren, die vollständig vom Hauptsystem getrennt ist und die Kerndienste ermöglicht und aufrechterhält, falls das Hauptbetriebssystem ausfällt. Gleichzeitig untersucht die Bank von England auch die Bereitschaft der Banken, der Bedrohung durch die Quantencomputertechnologie zu begegnen, die das Potenzial hat, die aktuellen Verschlüsselungsstandards zu stören und weitreichende Störungen bei Finanzzahlungs- und Clearingsystemen zu verursachen. Das könnte Sie interessieren. Die Warnung der Bank von England erfolgt zeitgleich mit einer ähnlichen Einschätzung des Internationalen Währungsfonds (IWF) in dieser Woche. Dieser erklärte, dass ein KI-gestützter Cyberangriff auf kritische Finanzinfrastrukturen das Vertrauen in das Währungssystem massiv untergraben könnte. Die Bank von England plant, die Ergebnisse ihrer branchenweiten Umfrage in Zusammenarbeit mit dem britischen Nationalen Zentrum für Cybersicherheit (NCSC) zu nutzen, um einen umfassenden systemweiten Reaktionsplan zu entwickeln. title: AI proves its worth in banking - 29 percent would rather talk to AI about sensitive money matters: EOS Group Reports
excerpt: 46 percent of European consumers report improved communication with their bank through AI. 29 percent would prefer speaking with AI rather than a human when discussing sensitive financial topics. 61 percent want proactive AI alerts to warn of potential account overdrafts. HAMBURG, Germany , Oct. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Personal advice has long been viewed as an essential part of banking relationships. This perception is shifting, as the latest EOS Banking AI Barometer reveals. The study examines how European consumers evaluate artificial intelligence in the banking sector. 46 percent report improved customer communication through AI support. Only 11 percent perceive a decline in service quality. Where technology genuinely helps, it is accepted. Nearly one in three respondents (29 percent) would prefer speaking with AI about sensitive banking matters rather than a human employee. Among 18-34-year-olds, this figure rises to 38 percent. However, the study indicates that AI still has limitations. Only 35 to 36 percent trust AI to understand their needs, act with precision, and solve problems effectively. Consumers show higher acceptance for information retrieval, speed, and availability. More than half of respondents (54 percent) value AI for helping them find information. Similarly, 51 percent praise faster communication and round-the-clock availability. Continue Reading. Despite these advantages, one key finding stands in contrast: 60 percent of respondents miss the human touch in AI communication. "46 percent of customers say service has improved through AI, only 11 percent perceive a decline. That is a clear signal for AI acceptance in customer service. But the 60 percent who miss the human element also tell us that AI alone is not the answer. The best banks use AI as a tool for better service, not as a replacement for relationships," says Marwin Ramcke, CEO of the EOS Group. From information agent to financial coach. Respondents identify potential for AI-powered customer service, particularly in financially challenging situations. "Our study reveals a clear direction in the use of AI services: customers are ready to move beyond reactive AI. They're seeking intelligent anticipation. 61 percent want alerts warning of potential overdrafts, and 51 percent value AI-powered payment plan suggestions when facing outstanding receivables," explains the CEO of the EOS Group. Consumers who have previously experienced payment difficulties are notably more open to AI-powered support services from banks than the general population. Rather than simply responding to customer inquiries, AI systems could proactively warn of financial risks and recommend tailored assistance. "Customers are ready for smarter services – banks just need to deliver," Ramcke concludes. About the study. For the EOS Banking AI Barometer study – How Europe really feels about AI in banking – 4,400 people in eleven European countries (Bulgaria, Croatia, France, Germany, Greece, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland, 400 respondents per country) were surveyed about their attitudes towards artificial intelligence in bank communications. The data was collected in July 2026, and the target group consisted of bank customers aged 18 to 65. The study was conducted online and was representative of the population. Find more information, infographics and downloads on the EOS Banking AI Barometer here. About the EOS Group. The EOS Group is a leading technology-driven investor in receivables portfolios and an expert in the processing of outstanding receivables. With over 50 years of experience and offices in more than 20 countries, EOS offers smart services for receivables management worldwide. Its key target sectors are banking, real estate, telecommunications, utilities, and e-commerce. EOS employs close to 6,000 people and is part of Otto Group. For more information on EOS Group: www. eos-solutions. com. Modal title.
